contrast: A false friend: Russian *драматически* suggests tragedy, but English *dramatically* usually just means *by a lot* — *sales rose dramatically* is good news. Compare *drastically*, which implies a severe and often unwelcome change.

senses.gloss: By a large amount, often suddenly.
examples: Prices have risen *dramatically* since spring.
Crime dropped *dramatically* after the new lights went in.
The weather changed *dramatically* overnight.

senses.gloss: In a theatrical, attention-seeking way.
examples: She sighed *dramatically* and left the room.
He paused *dramatically* before the last line.

contrast: Stronger and more negative than *dramatically*: *drastically* suggests harsh measures or a change for the worse (*drastically reduced staff*), while *dramatically* is neutral about whether the change is good.

senses.gloss: In an extreme way that has a large and serious effect.
examples: The company *drastically* cut its travel budget.
Rents have gone up *drastically* in this neighborhood.
Things could have gone *drastically* wrong.

senses.gloss: In an irregular, unpredictable way.
examples: The car was swerving *erratically* across both lanes.
His heart had been beating *erratically* all night.
The old printer works *erratically* at best.

contrast: *loose* /luːs/ rhymes with *goose*; *lose* /luːz/ is a different word, and *losely* does not exist. Sense 2 is almost always before a participle: *loosely based on*, *loosely translated*.

senses.gloss: Not tightly or firmly.
examples: Tie the rope *loosely* around the post.
Her hair hung *loosely* over her shoulders.

senses.gloss: Not exactly; in an approximate or free way.
examples: The movie is *loosely* based on a true story.
People use the word *loosely* to mean any kind of app.

type: place — on the internet; also manner
position: end — after the verb and its object
form: flat — the same form as the adjective *online*
contrast: No preposition before it: *buy online*, *meet online*, never ✗ *in online* or ✗ *in the online*. *Go online* means *connect to the internet*. Written as one word; the older *on-line* is now rare.

senses.gloss: On or through the internet.
examples: I bought the tickets *online*.
She works *online* from her kitchen table.
More people shop *online* now than in stores.

ru: офлайн, без подключения к интернету; отдельно, в частном порядке
type: place — not on the internet; also manner
position: end — after the verb and its object
form: flat — the same form as the adjective *offline*
contrast: Sense 2 is office jargon: *take it offline* means *talk about it later, just the people involved*, and has nothing to do with the internet.

senses.gloss: Without a connection to the internet.
examples: You can read the articles *offline* on the plane.
The app still works *offline*.
The server went *offline* just before noon.

senses.gloss: Privately, outside the current meeting or call.
examples: Let's discuss that *offline*.
We took the budget question *offline* after the call.

position: end — or after a noun: *fans worldwide*
form: flat — the same form as the adjective *worldwide*

senses.gloss: Throughout the world.
senses.ru: по всему миру, во всём мире
examples: The film earned nine hundred million dollars *worldwide*.
The company now ships *worldwide*.
Millions of viewers *worldwide* watched the launch.

position: after its word — after a noun phrase with *no* or *any*
contrast: Only in negatives, questions, and after *any*, and always **after** the noun phrase: *no idea whatsoever*, never ✗ *whatsoever no idea*. It is a stronger, more formal *at all*.

senses.gloss: At all — used after a noun phrase to strengthen a negative.
examples: I have no interest *whatsoever* in politics.
There's no evidence *whatsoever* that it works.
Did he give any reason *whatsoever*?

contrast: *At first* always implies that something changed later. To order steps or points, use *first* or *firstly*: ✗ *At first, preheat the oven* → *First, preheat the oven*. Russian *сначала* covers both, which is why the error is so common.

senses.gloss: At the beginning, in contrast with what happened later.
examples: *At first* I didn't like the city.
It was hard *at first*, but it got easier.
*At first* she thought it was a joke.

senses.gloss: At some time in the future, and certainly.
examples: *Sooner or later* you'll have to tell her.
Everyone gets caught *sooner or later*.
He knew *sooner or later* the money would run out.

contrast: The *on* is required: ✗ *from now I will* sounds unfinished, and ✗ *since now* is not English. For a date, use *starting* or *from … on*: *starting Monday*, *from Monday on*.

senses.gloss: Starting now and continuing into the future.
examples: *From now on*, I'm walking to work.
*From now on*, all requests go through Maria.
Things will be different *from now on*.

contrast: *For now* means *temporarily*; *by now* means *already, by this time* (*She should be home by now*). Neither is the same as *now*.

senses.gloss: For the present time, though this may change later.
examples: That's all *for now*.
Let's leave it here *for now*.
*For now*, the plan is to wait and see.

position: end — after the verb and its object
contrast: The standard preposition is *by*. *On accident* is common in the speech of younger Americans but is still considered nonstandard in writing; never ✗ *in accident*. The opposite is *on purpose*.

senses.gloss: Without intending to.
examples: I deleted the file *by accident*.
We met *by accident* at the airport.
She found the letter *by accident* while cleaning.

position: front or end — also mid after the subject
contrast: *As a result* links a sentence to the previous one, so it needs a period or semicolon before it, not just a comma. *As a result of* + noun is a preposition: *as a result of the storm*.

senses.gloss: Because of what has just been mentioned.
examples: The road was closed. *As a result*, we were an hour late.
He trained all winter and, *as a result*, won easily.
Sales fell, and two stores closed *as a result*.

contrast: *At the moment* means *now*; *in a moment* means *soon*; *in the moment* means *fully focused on the present*. Usually with a present tense, often the present progressive.

senses.gloss: Now; at the present time.
examples: She's in a meeting *at the moment*.
*At the moment* we have no plans to move.
I'm not working *at the moment*.

contrast: Like *ago*, it takes the simple past, never the present perfect: ✗ *I have met him long ago*. For something still true, use *for a long time*: *I have lived here for a long time*.

senses.gloss: A long time in the past.
examples: They moved away *long ago*.
*Long ago*, this whole valley was farmland.
I stopped worrying about that *long ago*.

position: any position — front with inversion, or mid
contrast: Fronted, it forces inversion like *never*: *Never again will I…*, not ✗ *Never again I will…*. In mid position the order is normal: *I will never again…*.

senses.gloss: Not at any time in the future.
examples: *Never again* will I fly that airline.
I'll *never again* lend him money.
She promised herself she would *never again* work weekends.

contrast: *For the first time* = the first occasion ever; *at first* = at the beginning, before a change; *first* = before anything else. Russian *впервые* is only the first of these.

senses.gloss: On the first occasion ever.
examples: I saw the ocean *for the first time* last summer.
*For the first time* in years, she took a real vacation.
He's cooking dinner *for the first time*, so be kind.

ru: как раз вовремя, в последний момент
contrast: *In time* means *early enough* (*in time for dinner*); *on time* means *at the scheduled time, not late* (*the train left on time*). *Just in time* is the close call.

senses.gloss: Only a moment before it would have been too late.
senses.ru: как раз вовремя, в последний момент
examples: We got to the gate *just in time*.
The ambulance arrived *just in time*.
She finished the slides *just in time* for the meeting.

contrast: *On and off* means exactly the same. Both describe an activity that keeps stopping and starting, not one that happens rarely — for that, use *occasionally*.

senses.gloss: Occasionally, with breaks in between.
examples: It rained *off and on* all day.
They've dated *off and on* for years.
I've been working on the book *off and on* since 2019.

contrast: Informal. *Like crazy* is the more common American equivalent and means the same. Neither suggests anger.

senses.gloss: Very fast, very hard, or very much.
examples: We ran *like mad* to catch the bus.
It's been snowing *like mad* since noon.
Everyone was working *like mad* before the deadline.
